Lidocaine and other local anaesthetic antiarrhythmics are specifically contraindicated because they add to the toxic burden. (Source: ANZCA and ASA: Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity)
source_refs: ANZCA and ASA: Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity

options.text: Give intravenous sodium bicarbonate and repeat the dose after five minutes
options.rationale: Sodium bicarbonate is the treatment for sodium channel blockade from tricyclic antidepressant poisoning and is a reasonable adjunct here, but it is not the specific antidote and should not be given first. The two poisonings share a mechanism but differ in the treatment with the strongest evidence. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

explanation.summary: Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity follows inadvertent intravascular injection or systemic absorption from a large volume block, and its incidence has fallen with ultrasound guidance but has not disappeared. The classic sequence begins with prodromal neurological symptoms including perioral numbness, metallic taste, tinnitus, visual disturbance and agitation, progresses to seizures, and then to cardiovascular toxicity with conduction delay, bradyarrhythmias, ventricular arrhythmias and asystole. Onset is typically within minutes but can be delayed for up to an hour with large volume blocks, so monitoring after the procedure matters. Management combines stopping the injection, airway and ventilation support, seizure control with a benzodiazepine, and lipid emulsion as the specific antidote. Adrenaline is used in reduced doses, propofol is avoided as a lipid substitute, and lidocaine and other sodium channel blocking antiarrhythmics are contraindicated. Prolonged resuscitation is justified because recovery after long arrests has been documented, and every clinician performing blocks should know where the lipid emulsion is kept.
key_points: Prodromal perioral numbness, metallic taste and tinnitus precede seizures and cardiac toxicity.
Onset can be delayed up to an hour after a large volume block.
Lipid emulsion 20 per cent is the specific antidote, given as a bolus then an infusion.
Adrenaline is used at markedly reduced doses and lidocaine is contraindicated.
Prolonged resuscitation is warranted because late recovery has been documented.
explanation.pearls: Keep a dedicated lipid emulsion kit wherever regional blocks are performed and rehearse the dose: 1.5 mL/kg of 20 per cent emulsion as a bolus followed by an infusion at 15 mL/kg/hour, with the bolus repeatable twice if circulation has not returned.

sources.label: ANZCA and ASA: Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity

subtopic_detail: exertional syncope in a young athlete with a murmur that increases on standing and lateral T wave inversion
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 19-year-old semi-professional footballer who blacked out twice in the last month, both times during sprinting at training. Each episode lasted under a minute with rapid full recovery and no confusion afterwards.

He has no chest pain and no palpitations, and he has never fainted while standing still or after standing up. His mother's brother died suddenly at 34 while jogging and no cause was found. On examination there is an ejection systolic murmur at the left sternal edge that becomes louder when he stands up from squatting and softer when he squats down. His electrocardiogram shows voltage criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy with deep T wave inversion in the lateral leads.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 58/min, blood pressure 122/76 mmHg with no postural drop, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Ejection systolic murmur at the left sternal edge louder on standing from squatting and softer on squatting, brisk carotid upstroke, no radiation to the carotids
data_table.Electrocardiogram: Voltage criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy with deep T wave inversion in leads V5, V6, I and aVL

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure him that exertional syncope in young athletes is usually benign
options.rationale: Syncope during rather than after exertion is a red flag for a structural or arrhythmic cardiac cause and is never reassured away, particularly with a family history of sudden death under 40. Post-exertional syncope on stopping is the pattern more often benign. (Source: CSANZ: Pre-participation screening and genetic heart disease)
source_refs: CSANZ: Pre-participation screening and genetic heart disease

options.text: Arrange an exercise stress test to reproduce the symptoms before imaging
options.rationale: Provoking symptoms in someone with suspected dynamic outflow obstruction risks the very event being investigated, and stress testing is done later, under supervision, for risk stratification once the anatomy is known. Imaging precedes provocation. (Source: CSANZ: Pre-participation screening and genetic heart disease)
source_refs: CSANZ: Pre-participation screening and genetic heart disease

options.text: Arrange transthoracic echocardiography and withhold competitive sport now
options.rationale: A murmur that increases when preload falls on standing, lateral T wave inversion with voltage criteria, exertional syncope and a family history of sudden death under 40 together require urgent imaging to define the myocardium and outflow tract. Sport is suspended immediately because the highest risk period is before the diagnosis is established, and continued training while awaiting a scan is what turns this presentation into a death. (Source: CSANZ: Pre-participation screening and genetic heart disease)
source_refs: CSANZ: Pre-participation screening and genetic heart disease

options.text: Start a beta blocker and allow training to continue while awaiting review
options.rationale: Beta blockade is a reasonable treatment once the diagnosis is confirmed and symptoms require it, but it does not abolish the risk of sudden arrhythmic death and allowing continued competition is the dangerous element of this option. Treatment follows diagnosis and risk stratification. (Source: CSANZ: Pre-participation screening and genetic heart disease)
source_refs: CSANZ: Pre-participation screening and genetic heart disease

options.text: Arrange a 24 hour Holter monitor alone and review the result in one month
options.rationale: Ambulatory monitoring contributes to risk stratification by detecting non-sustained ventricular tachycardia, but it cannot show the structural abnormality and a normal recording would be falsely reassuring. It is part of the assessment after imaging rather than instead of it. (Source: CSANZ: Pre-participation screening and genetic heart disease)
source_refs: CSANZ: Pre-participation screening and genetic heart disease

explanation.summary: Syncope occurring during exertion, as opposed to immediately after stopping, is a cardinal warning sign that demands assessment before any return to sport. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is the commonest inherited cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes and produces a dynamic outflow murmur that behaves opposite to the murmur of aortic stenosis: it increases when preload or afterload falls, as on standing or during Valsalva, and decreases when preload rises with squatting or handgrip. Electrocardiographic abnormalities precede symptoms in most cases, with deep lateral T wave inversion and voltage criteria being typical, and a completely normal tracing makes the diagnosis unlikely. Echocardiography defines wall thickness, outflow gradient and systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve, with cardiac magnetic resonance imaging used when windows are poor or apical disease is suspected. Family screening of first degree relatives is mandatory, and risk stratification determines whether an implantable defibrillator is required.
key_points: Syncope during exertion is a red flag, unlike syncope after stopping exercise.
The murmur increases on standing and Valsalva and decreases on squatting.
Deep lateral T wave inversion with voltage criteria is the typical electrocardiographic pattern.
Competitive sport is suspended pending diagnosis, not after it.
First degree relatives require clinical and electrocardiographic screening.
explanation.pearls: Any family history of sudden death under 40, including a death attributed to drowning, a single vehicle accident or unexplained epilepsy, should be treated as a possible inherited arrhythmia syndrome and triggers screening of the whole first degree family.

sources.label: CSANZ: Pre-participation screening and genetic heart disease

subtopic_detail: progressive breathlessness with a large inspiratory fall in systolic pressure and low voltage complexes in advanced malignancy
stem:
You are the oncology registrar called to see a 64-year-old woman with metastatic lung adenocarcinoma who has become breathless over five days and cannot lie flat.

She is sitting forward and is anxious. Her jugular venous pressure is visible at the angle of the jaw at 45 degrees and rises further on inspiration. Her heart sounds are quiet and her chest is clear on auscultation with no crackles. Measuring her blood pressure carefully, the systolic falls by 16 mmHg during inspiration. Her electrocardiogram shows small complexes throughout with beat to beat variation in QRS amplitude, and her chest radiograph shows an enlarged globular cardiac silhouette with clear lung fields. A bedside echocardiogram shows a large circumferential pericardial effusion with diastolic collapse of the right atrium.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 124/min, blood pressure 92/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 28/min, SpO2 94% in room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Jugular venous pressure elevated and rising on inspiration, quiet heart sounds, chest clear on auscultation, cool peripheries with capillary refill 3 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram with low voltage complexes and beat to beat QRS amplitude variation, chest radiograph with globular cardiac silhouette and clear lung fields, echocardiogram with large circumferential pericardial effusion and diastolic right atrial collapse

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give intravenous frusemide 40 mg and reassess the breathlessness later
options.rationale: Diuresis reduces the filling pressure that is maintaining cardiac output against external compression and can precipitate shock. It is the correct treatment for the pulmonary oedema this presentation mimics, which is excluded by the clear chest and clear lung fields. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Start a glyceryl trinitrate infusion to reduce the pulmonary congestion
options.rationale: Vasodilatation reduces preload and systemic vascular resistance, both of which are supporting circulation in tamponade, so it risks cardiovascular collapse. Nitrates are appropriate for acute pulmonary oedema with a raised blood pressure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Start high dose dexamethasone and arrange radiotherapy for the tumour
options.rationale: Corticosteroid and radiotherapy have a role in malignant airway or superior vena caval obstruction, but they do nothing for the mechanical problem of fluid under pressure in the pericardial sac. Drainage must come first regardless of the underlying tumour. (Source: eviQ: Oncological emergencies)

options.text: Arrange urgent echocardiography guided pericardiocentesis and drainage
options.rationale: An elevated jugular venous pressure that rises on inspiration, quiet heart sounds, an inspiratory systolic fall above 10 mmHg and diastolic right atrial collapse establish tamponade, which is relieved only by removing the fluid. Echocardiographic guidance with a drain left in place reduces complications and reaccumulation, which is common in malignant effusions. (Source: eviQ: Oncological emergencies)

options.text: Arrange computed tomography of the chest before any further treatment
options.rationale: Cross sectional imaging adds staging information but delays decompression while the patient sits at the steep part of the pressure volume curve, where small further increases in fluid cause abrupt collapse. Imaging follows stabilisation. (Source: eviQ: Oncological emergencies)

explanation.summary: Cardiac tamponade is a clinical diagnosis supported by echocardiography rather than a purely echocardiographic one, and in malignancy it often develops gradually, allowing the pericardium to stretch until a critical volume is reached and decompensation becomes abrupt. The physical signs reflect equalisation of diastolic pressures and exaggerated ventricular interdependence: a raised jugular venous pressure with preserved or exaggerated inspiratory rise, quiet heart sounds, tachycardia, hypotension and an inspiratory fall in systolic pressure greater than 10 mmHg. Electrocardiographic low voltage with beat to beat amplitude variation reflects the heart swinging within the fluid. The management principle is that anything reducing preload is harmful, so diuretics, nitrates and positive pressure ventilation are avoided, while cautious fluid loading can temporise in a hypovolaemic patient. Definitive treatment is drainage, and because malignant effusions reaccumulate, a drain is usually left in place with consideration of a pericardial window or sclerosant for recurrence. Fluid is sent for cytology, which also has staging implications.
key_points: Tamponade is a clinical diagnosis confirmed rather than made by echocardiography.
An inspiratory systolic fall above 10 mmHg is a key physical sign.
Diuretics, nitrates and positive pressure ventilation all reduce preload and are harmful.
Echocardiography guided drainage with a catheter left in place is the treatment.
Malignant effusions frequently reaccumulate and may need a window or sclerosant.
explanation.pearls: Chest radiograph enlargement of the cardiac silhouette requires roughly 200 mL or more of pericardial fluid, so a normal sized heart never excludes tamponade when fluid has accumulated rapidly after a procedure or trauma.

subtopic_detail: headache and nausea in several members of a household that improve away from home, with normal pulse oximetry
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 35-year-old woman with three days of throbbing headache, nausea and dizziness. It is the middle of a cold winter.

She tells you that both of her housemates have the same headache and one vomited this morning, and that all three feel better by the middle of the day at work and worse again a few hours after they get home. Their unflued gas heater in the living room has been running each evening since the cold weather started, and one housemate noticed sooty marks on the wall above it. She has no neck stiffness, no photophobia, no rash and no fever. Her neurological examination is normal and her pulse oximeter reads 99 per cent in room air.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96/min, blood pressure 124/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert and oriented, no neck stiffness or photophobia, normal fundoscopy, normal neurological examination, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Venous lactate 2.8 mmol/L (<2.0), full blood count and electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give intravenous fluids and metoclopramide for a presumed viral illness
options.rationale: A viral illness does not remit at work and recur at home, and it would not affect three adults with a time course tied to the evenings. Symptomatic treatment here would send her back into the exposure that caused the illness. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Carbon monoxide)
source_refs: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Carbon monoxide

options.text: Arrange computed tomography of the brain before any specific treatment
options.rationale: Imaging is indicated for focal neurology, altered conscious state or thunderclap onset, none of which is present, and it delays a treatment that is safe to start immediately. Scanning is reasonable later if symptoms fail to resolve with treatment. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Carbon monoxide)
source_refs: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Carbon monoxide

options.text: Give sumatriptan and advise review if the headaches persist next week
options.rationale: Triptans treat migraine, which does not spread to housemates or follow the geography of a house. Discharging her with an analgesic returns three people to an ongoing source of exposure that can be lethal during sleep. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Carbon monoxide)
source_refs: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Carbon monoxide

options.text: Arrange lumbar puncture after imaging to exclude subarachnoid bleeding
options.rationale: Subarachnoid haemorrhage presents with sudden severe headache in one person, not with three days of building symptoms shared by a household. The shared exposure history is what redirects the workup. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Carbon monoxide)
source_refs: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Carbon monoxide

options.text: Give high flow oxygen by non rebreather mask and take a blood gas sample
options.rationale: Headache and nausea affecting a whole household, worse at home and better away from it, with an unflued combustion heater and soot staining, is carbon monoxide exposure, and treatment is 100 per cent oxygen through a non rebreather mask started before any confirmatory result. A blood gas analysed by co-oximetry is required because standard pulse oximetry cannot distinguish carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin and reads falsely normal. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Carbon monoxide)
source_refs: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Carbon monoxide

explanation.summary: Carbon monoxide poisoning is the great imitator of winter emergency medicine, presenting with headache, nausea, dizziness, fatigue and confusion that are routinely attributed to viral illness or migraine. Three features should redirect the assessment: more than one person in a household affected, symptoms that improve away from the building and recur on return, and the presence of an unflued or poorly maintained combustion appliance, which in Australia has caused deaths in both rental housing and camping situations with fuel burning devices in enclosed spaces. Standard pulse oximetry is falsely reassuring because it cannot distinguish carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin, so a blood gas with co-oximetry is required, and the level correlates poorly with symptom severity. Treatment is high flow oxygen, which reduces the elimination half life from several hours in room air to around an hour, continued until symptoms resolve and the level normalises. Hyperbaric therapy is considered for loss of consciousness, neurological signs, myocardial ischaemia, very high levels or pregnancy, and every case requires public health notification and remediation of the source before anyone returns to the building.
key_points: Multiple household members affected with symptoms tied to being at home is the key pattern.
Pulse oximetry reads falsely normal, so co-oximetry on a blood gas is required.
High flow oxygen is started before confirmation and shortens the elimination half life substantially.
Levels correlate poorly with severity, so treatment follows the clinical picture.
The source must be identified and remediated before anyone returns to the premises.
explanation.pearls: Ask explicitly whether the family pet has also been unwell, since small animals with high metabolic rates develop symptoms earlier than people and a sick cat or bird at home is often the first clue to a domestic exposure.

sources.label: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Carbon monoxide

subtopic_detail: day three assessment of response to intravenous corticosteroid in an acute severe colitis admission
stem:
You are the gastroenterology registrar reviewing a 28-year-old woman on day three of an admission with ulcerative colitis. She came in with nine bloody stools a day, cramping and fatigue, and has been on intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg four times daily since admission.

Today she reports seven bloody stools in the last 24 hours, including two overnight. Her abdomen is soft with mild tenderness and no guarding, and bowel sounds are present. Stool testing for Clostridioides difficile and enteric pathogens is negative, and sigmoidoscopy on admission showed deep ulceration without cytomegalovirus inclusions on biopsy. Her abdominal radiograph today shows a transverse colon diameter of 4 cm with no free gas. She has had no previous biologic therapy and her tuberculosis and hepatitis screening sent on admission are negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 98/min, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 37.4 °C
data_table.Investigations: C-reactive protein 52 mg/L (<5, was 68 on admission), haemoglobin 98 g/L (115-155), albumin 28 g/L (35-50), stool testing negative for Clostridioides difficile and enteric pathogens, transverse colon diameter 4 cm on abdominal radiograph
data_table.Medications: Intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg four times daily since admission, enoxaparin prophylaxis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management now?

options.text: Start rescue therapy with infliximab and involve the colorectal surgeons
options.rationale: More than eight stools a day on day three, or three to eight stools with a C-reactive protein above 45 mg/L, predicts a high likelihood of colectomy during that admission and defines failure of intravenous corticosteroid. Rescue therapy with infliximab or ciclosporin is started at that point, with concurrent surgical review so that a timely operation follows if rescue fails. (Source: GESA: Acute severe ulcerative colitis)

options.text: Continue intravenous corticosteroid for a further five days and reassess
options.rationale: Continuing beyond day three in a non-responder delays rescue therapy and surgery, and prolonged corticosteroid exposure increases postoperative complications if colectomy becomes necessary. Response is formally assessed on day three precisely to prevent this drift. (Source: GESA: Acute severe ulcerative colitis)

options.text: Switch to oral prednisolone 40 mg daily and plan discharge in two days
options.rationale: Stepping down to oral therapy is appropriate for a patient who has responded, with stool frequency falling and inflammatory markers normalising. Discharging a patient still passing seven bloody stools a day risks readmission with perforation. (Source: GESA: Acute severe ulcerative colitis)

options.text: Start oral mesalazine at maximal dose and continue the corticosteroid
options.rationale: Aminosalicylates maintain remission and treat mild to moderate disease but have no role in acute severe colitis, where they do not alter the trajectory. They are reintroduced once the acute episode is controlled. (Source: GESA: Acute severe ulcerative colitis)

options.text: Start oral loperamide to reduce stool frequency and continue the steroid
options.rationale: Antimotility agents are avoided in acute severe colitis because they can precipitate toxic megacolon by masking the very stool frequency used to judge response. They remain useful in quiescent disease with functional diarrhoea. (Source: GESA: Acute severe ulcerative colitis)

explanation.summary: Acute severe ulcerative colitis is defined by six or more bloody stools a day with evidence of systemic upset, and it remains a condition with real mortality, so admissions are managed jointly by gastroenterology and colorectal surgery from day one. Intravenous corticosteroid is first line, along with venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, correction of anaemia and electrolytes, exclusion of superimposed Clostridioides difficile and cytomegalovirus infection, and avoidance of opioids, antimotility agents and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. The day three assessment is the pivot of the admission: persisting high stool frequency, or intermediate frequency with a raised C-reactive protein, identifies patients who will not respond and who need rescue therapy with infliximab or ciclosporin. Rescue therapy is itself assessed at around day seven, and failure at that point means colectomy. Daily abdominal examination and radiographs when there is concern about dilatation are essential, since colonic dilatation beyond 5.5 cm, perforation or massive haemorrhage mandate immediate surgery regardless of the medical plan.
key_points: Acute severe colitis is six or more bloody stools daily with systemic upset.
Response to intravenous corticosteroid is formally assessed on day three.
More than eight stools daily, or three to eight with C-reactive protein above 45 mg/L, predicts colectomy.
Rescue therapy is infliximab or ciclosporin, with surgical involvement in parallel.
Opioids, antimotility drugs and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs are avoided throughout.
explanation.pearls: Colonic diameter above 5.5 cm on abdominal radiograph, or any free gas, converts this from a medical problem to an immediate surgical one, so repeat the film whenever stool frequency falls at the same time as abdominal distension increases, which is the deceptive pattern of evolving toxic megacolon.

subtopic_detail: confusion in an older woman with a near normal pH concealing a high anion gap acidosis and a respiratory alkalosis
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 72-year-old woman brought in by her son with four days of increasing confusion. He says she has been complaining that her ears are ringing and has been breathing oddly since yesterday.

She takes aspirin 300 mg four times daily, bought over the counter for shoulder pain, and her son thinks she has also been taking a powder from the chemist for the same pain. She is agitated, disoriented to time and place, sweaty and febrile at 38.1 °C, with deep rapid respirations. Her chest is clear, there is no neck stiffness or rash, and her neurological examination shows no focal deficit. She has taken no deliberate overdose according to her son, and her regular tablets are all accounted for.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 112/min, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 34/min, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 38.1 °C
data_table.Investigations: pH 7.41 (7.35-7.45), pCO2 22 mmHg (35-45), bicarbonate 14 mmol/L (22-32), anion gap 22 mmol/L (8-16), sodium 141 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), glucose 3.8 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), lactate 2.4 mmol/L (<2.0), creatinine 128 micromol/L (60-110), salicylate 3.9 mmol/L (therapeutic 1.1-2.2)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Give activated charcoal and repeat the drug level in six hours time
options.rationale: Charcoal is useful for recent large ingestions and for ongoing absorption from concretions, but it does nothing for drug already distributed into tissue over four days of accumulation. Using it as the sole measure in a confused patient also risks aspiration. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Give sodium bicarbonate with potassium and arrange urgent haemodialysis
options.rationale: Chronic salicylate toxicity with altered mental status is an indication for haemodialysis regardless of the absolute level, and alkalinisation with sodium bicarbonate is started immediately because raising serum and urinary pH keeps salicylate ionised, out of the brain and excreted by the kidney. Potassium must be replaced in the same fluid, since hypokalaemia prevents the kidney from excreting bicarbonate and defeats the alkalinisation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Intubate and ventilate for airway protection given her confusion now
options.rationale: Intubation is the classic trap in this poisoning, because her hyperventilation is the compensation keeping her pH survivable, and any period of apnoea or conventional ventilator settings precipitates a catastrophic fall in pH that drives salicylate into the brain. If intubation is unavoidable, it is done with bicarbonate loading and very high minute ventilation matched to her own. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Give intravenous fluid alone and monitor her conscious state closely
options.rationale: Volume replacement is necessary because these patients are markedly dehydrated, but fluid alone does not enhance elimination and observation wastes the window in which neurological injury is preventable. Fluid is a component of the correct plan rather than the whole of it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Give intravenous acetylcysteine and admit for overnight observation
options.rationale: Acetylcysteine is the antidote for paracetamol poisoning, which is worth excluding given the additional chemist powder, but it has no role against this drug. Confusing the two analgesic poisonings is a recognised error when a patient has been taking several over the counter products. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

explanation.summary: Chronic salicylate toxicity occurs in older patients taking regular over the counter analgesia and is frequently missed because there is no history of overdose and the presentation resembles sepsis, delirium or a respiratory illness. Salicylate stimulates the respiratory centre, producing a primary respiratory alkalosis, and uncouples oxidative phosphorylation, producing a high anion gap metabolic acidosis with fever, sweating and hypoglycaemia, particularly in the brain where cerebrospinal fluid glucose can be low despite a normal serum value. Because the two disturbances oppose each other, the pH can be near normal, so the diagnosis rests on recognising the anion gap and the low carbon dioxide rather than on the pH. Chronic toxicity causes neurological injury at much lower levels than acute overdose, so dialysis criteria are correspondingly lower and altered mental status alone justifies it. Management is alkalinisation with sodium bicarbonate and generous potassium, volume replacement, glucose supplementation even when the serum glucose is normal, and avoidance of intubation wherever possible.
key_points: A near normal pH with a high anion gap and a low carbon dioxide indicates a mixed disorder.
Chronic toxicity produces neurological injury at far lower levels than acute overdose.
Altered mental status is an indication for dialysis regardless of the measured level.
Alkalinisation fails without adequate potassium replacement.
Intubation removes the compensatory hyperventilation and can be rapidly fatal.
explanation.pearls: Give glucose to any salicylate poisoned patient with altered mental status even when the serum glucose is normal, because cerebral glucose use is uncoupled from the serum level and neuroglycopenia occurs with normal peripheral readings.
